The good news is, you can fix the issue with your dog fairly simply/easily--when we "inherited" our senior lab, she was ten or twenty pounds overweight, too, but she lost it fairly quickly. If you're not already, switch to a food for Senior Dogs, preferably one with glucosamine & chondroitin. Senior foods usually have fewer calories. If your dog doesn't start eating again soon--he will, when he's hungry enough, but I know it's a pain in the ass--see if your food brand makes a canned version. Mix half a can with the dry food, and gradually phase the cans out. (Or keep the cans, if you want.) Or try doing things like boiling some cheep beef cuts, bone-in if you can get them, (no salt!) in enough water to cover; when the beef is all cooked and the bones empty of marrow, chop up the meat and discard the bones (do NOT give them to the dog; they will be super brittle). Refrigerate the meat. Keep simmering the liquid to reduce it a bit, and then put it in a container in the fridge.

Every time you feed your dog, moisten the food with a bit of the beef stock you made. Add a little of the chopped meat, if you like. Eventually, as with the canned food, you start adding less and less of the stock.

It seems like a pain in the ass, I know, especially with a new baby. But since you're not making a stock for human consumption, you literally just throw some cheap beef in a pot; you don't have to chop up carrots and onions or make a bouquet garni or dig the peppercorns out of the pantry, and you won't have to skim the top or strain it all or worry about separating the fat (though refrigerating it will do that for you anyway). So really the only effort it requires is pouring water into a pot and turning on a burner, and then shredding the meat seven or eight hours later.

If you don't want to do that, of course, you can look for a canned beef stock or use Better Than Bouillon or similar (check the ingredients, though, because dogs shouldn't have onions). The point is just to have a flavorful liquid without a lot of calories to add to the food, to make it more appetizing.

And yes, it is! I mean, I did have my husband, but he had to work, too--he only got like a week off for the new baby--so it was mostly just me by myself at home, and it was scary as shit. I had never even spent time near a baby before, much less had the exclusive 24/7 care of one. Everyone tells you to sleep when the baby sleeps, but I was so afraid of something happening to her that I couldn't (and it didn't help that a few family members would come by to see the baby, and they would always come just as she fell asleep, and they would sit there telling me to sleep when the baby sleeps and I'm like, "She's sleeping now, but you know, you're here..." [of course, I didn't actually say that, but I thought it, lol].)

IMO the first three months are the hardest. Once you get to that point they start sleeping better (generally) and you're more familiar with their rhythms and needs and such, and more comfortable overall. They "wake up" a little then, too, and start to be more fun in terms of interacting with you. But yeah, it's so hard at first. One thing I used to do is keep a cloth--you know, one of those little baby towels/blankets you come home from the hospital with--on me all day, and when we'd put her down to sleep in her bassinet we'd tuck that cloth over the mattress, so she could smell me while she was sleeping. It really helped her sleep.

She was a formula baby (I didn't have enough milk, so gave up after about ten days; I was all scabbed and nursing was so painful), so we would pre-prep bottles for her--we'd fill one with water to the right level, put it in the microwave, and set the timer for ten seconds or whatever. So when she wanted to be fed, especially in the middle of the night, all we had to do was hit the "Start" button and get out enough powder, and mix it in. (They say don't microwave formula, and they're right, but if you micro just the water, it gets shaken up enough before and after adding the formula that you don't have to worry about "hot spots." My best friend (whose toddlers I watch) just trained hers to accept room-temp formula & breastmilk--she nursed both of hers, and I nursed our second for 17 months, but we both gave one formula or expressed milk bottle per day to give ourselves a break, lol. When we went out I'd take a frozen breastmilk bottle from the fridge and hold it between my thighs in the car to thaw & warm it, so by the time we got to where we were going it was basically body temp.

The main thing to remember is, whatever you're doing, you're doing it right. As long as your baby isn't starving or sitting around in a filthy diaper for hours on end, you're fine. I know it's painful and awful to hear them cry, but it's not going to kill them to cry; you can take five minutes to hop in the shower or eat a sandwich or even step outside (while they are safely strapped into a swing or seat or whatever) to get some fresh air/calm down if you're getting stressed, and it's not going to hurt them. This is your baby; you don't have to do what other people tell you to do, if you and he like doing it a different way. And all babies are different, so what people tell you that you must or must not do doesn't necessarily apply. Our oldest didn't like the baby carrier (you know, like a backpack on your front that holds baby); our youngest loved it. Our youngest refused to be put down and would scream and cry if she wasn't being held--oh how she hated the carseat, and screamed and screamed--our oldest fell asleep almost instantly in the car, and was perfectly happy in her swing or bassinet. Oldest loved her "dummy" (pacifier), youngest never took one. Some babies sleep, and some don't; there's no "One size fits all," or one thing that absolutely works with every baby, so just do what feels natural and right to you, and if you're getting stressed or upset, take a minute for yourself--he will survive, and so will you.

In other words: you're doing fine. :-)
